evidence.claim: A river road became Washington’s first scenic byway, with room to slow down
evidence.quote: The canyon route had been designated as the state's first scenic byway in 1967, following the enactment of the system, and was provisionally numbered and signed as State Route 821. A lower speed limit of 45 miles per hour (72 km/h) was also set on the highway to discourage use by trucks and encourage scenic touring.

evidence.claim: The Yakima River Canyon Scenic Byway follows the river’s bends beneath basalt cliffs between Ellensburg and Selah.
evidence.quote: It runs for 25 miles (40 km) through the Yakima Canyon, following the meandering Yakima River between Selah and Ellensburg.

evidence.claim: beneath basalt cliffs
evidence.quote: Pass by rugged basalt cliffs towering above the river

evidence.claim: Two lanes run along the canyon bottom, with shoulders only in places.
evidence.quote: SR 821 generally consists of two lanes with a width of 11 feet (3.4 m), with occasional shoulders

evidence.claim: State of Washington Tourism allows one hour for its 27-mile scenic trip.
evidence.quote: Length 27 Miles | 43 KM Drive Time 1 Hour

evidence.claim: Designated in 1967 as Washington’s first scenic byway, the corridor was proposed, Governor Daniel J. Evans explained, to let travelers appreciate the landscape at a slower pace.
evidence.quote: The Yakima River Canyon Scenic Byway (YRCSB) “was proposed as the state’s first scenic corridor due to its great potential for allowing the traveler to pass through beautiful country at a pace enabling him to enjoy and appreciate its beauty” (Daniel J. Evans, Governor).

evidence.claim: Designated in 1967 as Washington’s first scenic byway
evidence.quote: The canyon route had been designated as the state's first scenic byway in 1967

evidence.claim: The state completed the canyon road in 1924 to replace a gravel route over the mountains to the west.
evidence.quote: The Yakima Canyon road was constructed in 1924 by the state government to replace a gravel road over the mountains to the west

evidence.claim: Crews blasted tunnels through basalt; when traffic outgrew them, a new alignment closer to the river bypassed the tunnels in 1963.
evidence.quote: The canyon highway's tunnels were bypassed by a new alignment built closer to the river in 1963, after traffic volumes had outgrown the narrow tunnels.

evidence.claim: Crews blasted tunnels through basalt
evidence.quote: included several tunnels cut through the lava basalt cliffs using dynamite that were later abandoned.

evidence.claim: I-82 later diverted through traffic, and US 97 moved onto the interstate in 1973, leaving the canyon road as SR 821.
evidence.quote: In 1973, US 97 was rerouted onto I-82 between Ellensburg and Yakima, while the old alignment through the canyon became SR 821.

evidence.claim: I-82 later diverted through traffic
evidence.quote: bypassing the congested highway through the Yakima River Canyon.

evidence.claim: The canyon highway had joined the federal US 97 route in 1926 and received concrete paving in 1932, before the narrow tunnels were bypassed.
evidence.quote: Under the federal system, the Ellensburg–Yakima section formed part of US 97, the main north–south route through central Washington and Oregon. The highway was paved with concrete in 1932
the federal numbered highway system created in 1926.

evidence.claim: Driving south from the Kittitas Valley, enter the canyon through hairpin turns in its narrowest stretch, then reach the footbridge at Umtanum Creek.
evidence.quote: Further north of the ranch is the parking lot for the Umtanum Creek Recreation Area, with a network of hiking trails connected via a footbridge over the Yakima River. After completing a series of hairpin turns along the narrowest section of the valley, SR 821 is rejoined by the railroad and enters the wide Kittitas Valley

evidence.claim: Continue along the river to Roza Dam, where the highway stays uphill while the railroad crosses the water.
evidence.quote: At Roza Dam, the railroad crosses over to the west side of the river while SR 821 stays uphill from the river, cutting through part of the ridge.

evidence.claim: Beyond the canyon’s passage through Umtanum Ridge, farms near Pomona lead toward Selah.
evidence.quote: The highway continues north through farms near the community of Pomona

evidence.claim: Beyond the canyon’s passage through Umtanum Ridge
evidence.quote: Near the south end of the Yakima River Canyon, which cuts across the Umtanum Ridge

evidence.claim: A footbridge across the Yakima River connects the Umtanum Creek parking area with a network of hiking trails.
evidence.quote: the parking lot for the Umtanum Creek Recreation Area, with a network of hiking trails connected via a footbridge over the Yakima River.

evidence.claim: It is one of five developed recreation sites managed by the Bureau of Land Management in the canyon.
evidence.quote: The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) operates five developed recreation sites and campground areas: Umtanum Creek, Lmuma Creek, Big Pines, Bighorn, and Roza.

evidence.claim: Here the road journey has a pedestrian crossing of its own, linking the highway side to trails across the water.
evidence.quote: the parking lot for the Umtanum Creek Recreation Area, with a network of hiking trails connected via a footbridge over the Yakima River.

evidence.claim: At Roza Dam, road and railroad take different sides of the river: the railway crosses west while SR 821 remains uphill.
evidence.quote: At Roza Dam, the railroad crosses over to the west side of the river while SR 821 stays uphill from the river, cutting through part of the ridge.

evidence.claim: The diversion dam was built in 1939, with a crest 486 feet long and a height of 67 feet.
evidence.quote: This gravity dam was built in 1939, is 486 feet (148 m) long at the crest and 67 feet (20 m) high

evidence.claim: Power generation came online in 1956.
evidence.quote: The dam also has 12.9 MW power production capacity, online as of 1956.

evidence.claim: Its adult fish ladder leads to a trap where fish are counted before release above the dam.
evidence.quote: There is also an adult fish ladder that collects fish in a trap, where they are counted and then released above the dam.

evidence.claim: Some wild fish are collected weekly as broodstock for the Cle Elum Supplementation and Research Facility.
evidence.quote: A portion of wild fish are collected weekly to use as broodstock for the Cle Elum Supplementation and Research Facility.

evidence.claim: The dam lies just west of SR 821, making this a meeting of highway, railway and river infrastructure.
evidence.quote: Roza Dam (National ID # WA00275) is a diversion dam on the Yakima River, about 10 miles (16 km) north of Yakima, just west of SR 821.

evidence.claim: Near the canyon’s southern end, the Yakima River cuts through Umtanum Ridge.
evidence.quote: Near the south end of the Yakima River Canyon, which cuts across the Umtanum Ridge

evidence.claim: This long ridge belongs to the Yakima Fold Belt, where Miocene Columbia River basalt flows were folded into east-trending ridges.
evidence.quote: Umtanum Ridge is part of the Yakima Fold Belt of east-tending long ridges formed by the folding of Miocene Columbia River basalt flows.

evidence.claim: The river’s crossing is called the Umtanum Ridge Water Gap.
evidence.quote: The Yakima River cuts through the ridge at the Umtanum Ridge Water Gap.

evidence.claim: Manastash Ridge parallels it to the north, and Yakima Ridge lies to the south.
evidence.quote: Umtanum Ridge is paralleled on the north by Manastash Ridge and on the south by Yakima Ridge.
